players.product: Data center leasing to hyperscalers and enterprises (Northern Virginia, Richmond, London, Amsterdam, Mumbai; ~325 MW of leasable capacity energizing over the next 24 months) plus hyperscale and neocloud data center decommissioning

quarterly_data.signal: CFO: 'This year, we'll do a little over $1 billion of revenue in data center, and the team has already signed contracts for data centers that we need to build and energize, which would grow the business another, call it 40%. Just with what we've already sold.' Significant additional land will be energized over the next few years. None of the 325 MW energizing over the next 18 to 24 months is leased ('All of that is incremental to our P&L'); it sits almost exclusively in tier 1 markets (Virginia, parts of Europe, India), the pipeline is deeper than historically with 'multiple parties interested in each one' of those buildings, and full-year leasing is expected to be 'meaningfully beyond' the 100 MW target. The CFO expects the growth portfolio (data center, ALM, digital) to keep growing 'north of 20% combined'.
quarterly_data.figure: data center revenue a little over $1 billion this year; signed contracts would grow it another, call it 40%

quarterly_data.signal: CFO on build and lease timing: Iron Mountain is 'not a speculative builder' and starts construction once it has a pre-lease; hyperscale pre-leases run '10, 15 years of duration' and clients generally lease '12 to 18 months before delivery'; it can 'build a data center in 9 to 10 months' in most geographies, with long lead time equipment already on order (generators and backup generators can carry '2, 3 year or beyond lead times'; cooling also long-lead), all on schedule with key vendors. Almost all leases are for core cloud or inference, and 'More and more of the pipeline is becoming AI-oriented inference': inference tenants want more density and liquid cooling, which raises the build price per megawatt and also the lease price.
quarterly_data.figure: pre-leases 12 to 18 months before delivery; build in 9 to 10 months; generator lead times 2, 3 years or beyond

quarterly_data.signal: Supplier Dominion Energy (utility power): CFO said the energization schedule is with utilities Iron Mountain knows well - it has operated in Virginia 'with Dominion Energy for years and years now, and they are the key utility for both the Richmond and the Manassas market'; 'We've previously been under deposit with them for certain long lead time elements that they need to build out the grid to support our future data center sites.' It also has utility relationships in Mumbai and Madrid. CFO: 'I feel highly confident in our ability to energize', while agreeing power is the industry's biggest governor.

CFO on data center pricing and renewals: the enterprise colocation book is 'ballpark a third of what we are operating', with mark-to-market and renewal spreads of 'double digit to even 20% compounded for the last three or so years' and low churn ('last year we were at sub 3% and kind of like 2% or so through the first nine months, 2.5%'). The first large single-tenant hyperscale lease came in about 2020-2021 and commenced in 2023; the weighted average lease expiration across the portfolio is 'north of 10 years'. Hyperscale contracts carry renewal options; CFO's guess is that with energy likely to stay a constraint 'it is going to be very advantageous for those clients to renew in the future'.
quarterly_data.figure: colo renewal spreads double digit to 20% compounded; churn sub 3% last year; weighted average lease expiration north of 10 years

quarterly_data.signal: CFO on Asset Lifecycle Management: ALM did '$30 million of revenue' in 2021 and is projected at 'approximately $1 billion' this year; the ALM TAM is '$35 billion estimated', 75% of it corporate clients. In hyperscale data center decommissioning, memory 'might be 50% or more' of the value of decommissioned gear; some memory SKUs have been 'up as much as 30%' and others down, and Q2 carried relatively more DDR3 versus more DDR4 in Q1; memory pricing has been 'stable to even slightly up' since the end of Q2. Hyperscale decommissioning is a revenue share model where Iron Mountain 'might get 20%' of the gear's sale price, with margins 'low double digit to high teens'; enterprise ALM is fee for service with margins 'mid-20s to 30s'.
quarterly_data.figure: ALM $30 million (2021) to approximately $1 billion (2026); ALM TAM $35 billion; memory 50% or more of decommissioned value; revenue share about 20%

quarterly_data.signal: Customer Department of the Treasury (digital solutions): CFO expected 'about $45 million of revenue' from the contract this year and is running ahead ('a couple of 2, 3 million ahead in the second quarter'), so 'We will probably exceed that level'; 'next year and for the years beyond, we expect to do at least $100 million of revenue on that business.' The contract was awarded to four potential partners, with Iron Mountain the largest; 100% of the theoretical volume would be 'about $150 million of revenue in any given year'. The digital solutions business runs at 'north of $600 million of revenue' annually (sub-$200 million not many years ago) and grew 20% in the most recent quarter. Records management: around 6% pricing benefit, physical volume up '20, 30, 40 basis points a year'.
quarterly_data.figure: Treasury contract about $45 million this year, at least $100 million next year; digital solutions north of $600 million, up 20%
